newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark edges up as broad EMU seen on track.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark edges up as broad EMU seen on track.

text.p: Sterling edged up within its recent ranges against the mark as the French government's deficit-cutting plans did nothing to scotch expectations of a broad-based European economic and monetary union.
French measures to cut the budget deficit by 0.4 percentage points of gross domestic product in 1997 would still leave the government with a deficit of between 3.1 and 3.3 percent.

This increases the chances that the EMU entry criteria will be diluted, and that countries with a shorter track record of economic stability than Germany will join in the planned launch of the European single currency in 1999.

"The combination of the audit and the package of measures will reinforce the market's belief that EMU is on track and that it will be broadly based," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan. "This implies the euro will be weak and is supportive for the dollar and sterling."
Sterling/mark was at 3.0085/95 at 1115 GMT from 2.9990/08 late Friday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6753/63 from $1.6770/80 on Friday.
Gains that sterling/mark made in the wake of the French deficit plans were in line with the dollar's advance against the mark rather than a sign of independent strength, analysts said.

"The pound is on the sidelines and following the direction of the dollar," said Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank of America. "It's struggling to go anywhere at the moment and will only get a boost if strong retail sales numbers on Wednesday put rate hikes back in focus."

Sterling has leapt to its strongest levels in nearly seven years in trade-weighted terms as talk of higher UK interest rates welded with the perception that the UK is a safe haven from concern about the stability of EMU.
But the toll this is taking on UK exporters could prove its undoing if data on Thursday shows the trade deficit widening.
Sterling strength is the biggest worry for British exporters, according to a quarterly survey by DHL published earlier today.

It showed 67 percent of the 1,004 exporters polled expect the pound's rise to have a negative impact on sales on a one-year view. Sixty-seven percent of those surveyed cited exchange rates as a cause for concern on a three-month horizon.
Most analysts are not looking for the pound to climb too much higher against other major currencies in the coming months, but nor do they expect any immediate relief for British exporters.
"Sterling's peak is in sight and it should not get much beyond 3.05 (marks)," said Persaud at JP Morgan. "But it is not going to fall dramatically anytime soon."
